title: 78 arrests as Hong Kong police bust underground ‘mini-casino’ and racecourse betting syndicate
summary:
Police have arrested 78 people during a Hong Kong Island anti-triad operation, targeting an underground “mini-casino” in North Point and a gang organising illegal racehorse betting.



Forty-two men and 36 women were arrested between July 7 and Monday, Vincent Lo, senior inspector of police said in a media briefing on Tuesday.



Happy Valley Racecourse. File photo: GovHK.



The arrestees were aged 16 to 68, with some having links to organised crime.



They were arrested on suspicion of various offences, including operating an illegal gambling establishment, gambling in an illegal gambling establishment, trafficking in a dangerous drug, claiming to be a member of a triad society, wounding, possession of an offensive weapon and money laundering.



Four illegal gambling dens and 10 premises offering illegal prostitution were dismantled, the police said, adding that they seized drugs worth around HK$500,000.



The raids were part of a joint anti-triad operation across Guangdong province, Hong Kong and Macau, Lo said.



Hong Kong Police Force. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



Lo said the “underground gambling den” in North Point was located within a ground-floor residential unit of about 1,000 square feet. It featured a mahjong and baccarat area, resembling a “mini-casino,” Lo said. 



“To attract nearby residents to stay and gamble, the den also provided three meals a day and beverages,” Lo said in Cantonese, adding that it is estimated that the operators saw a maximum monthly income of around HK$400,000.



Illegal betting inside Happy Valley Racecourse



Police also dismantled a criminal syndicate which organised illegal bets on horse racing inside the Hong Kong Jockey Club’s (HKJC) Happy Valley Racecourse.



After receiving a report from the HKJC saying it suspected there were cases of illegal betting at its racecourse, the police investigated and took action on the race day of July 8. They arrested one Hong Kong…

title: China summons Philippine ambassador over clash in disputed waters
summary:
China summoned the Philippine ambassador on Tuesday following a clash at a disputed shoal in the South China Sea, which sparked condemnation of Beijing by Manila’s allies.



The Philippine military accused the China Coast Guard of clubbing a Filipino sailor with a baton on Monday, July 20, 2026. Photo: Philippines Coast Guard.



Beijing claims sovereignty over almost the entire South China Sea, a vital global trade route, despite an international ruling that found its claims have no legal basis.



Multiple nations in the region, including the Philippines, have territorial claims that overlap with China’s, and altercations regularly occur in the heavily patrolled waterway.



The Philippine military accused the China Coast Guard of clubbing a Filipino sailor with a baton on Monday as they approached a grounded vessel that has long served as a Philippine garrison.




WATCH: Philippine Navy personnel aboard rubber boats deployed from BRP Sierra Madre conducted a lawful and non-confrontational operation to drive away a China Coast Guard RHIB that had unlawfully approached the vicinity of the outpost within waters where the Philippines exercises… pic.twitter.com/Cz4QuR2OKG— Armed Forces of the Philippines (@TeamAFP) July 21, 2026




China’s foreign ministry said Tuesday it had “urgently summoned” the Philippine ambassador “to lodge solemn representations over the Philippines’ deliberate provocation and attack… at Ren’ai Reef”, referring to a flashpoint also known as the Second Thomas Shoal.



“The Philippine side provoked first, yet it has turned the blame upside down, distorted the facts, and maliciously hyped the issue,” the foreign ministry said in a statement.



The Philippine military accused the China Coast Guard of clubbing a Filipino sailor with a baton on Monday, July 20, 2026. Photo: Philippines Coast Guard.

title: Hong Kong High Court judge Wilson Chan caught plagiarising in judgement for third time
summary:
A Hong Kong judge previously reprimanded for plagiarism has been caught copying again, making it the third known incident over the past three years.



High Court Judge Wilson Chan. Photo: Judiciary. 



High Court judge Wilson Chan was accused by the plaintiff in a case he presided over of lifting the defendant’s opening and closing arguments. Those paragraphs comprised 95 per cent of the judgement he delivered, local media reported on Monday.



The case related to a dispute between Koo Ming-kown, the founder of digital products company Nam Tai Electronics, and his former brother-in-law. Koo had sued his brother-in-law for not giving up HK$40 million in shares.



After Koo lost the case, he filed an appeal, stating that Chan had copied large parts of his brother-in-law’s submissions, as he questioned whether the judge had properly analysed the case.



Hong Kong’s High Court on November 11, 2024. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



The Court of Appeal sided with Koo last week, ordering a retrial before a different judge.



‘Judicial copying’



Chan, who presided over the early proceedings of the 47 democrats national security case, has been caught plagiarising at least twice before.



Great Eagle Holdings. File photo: Leasing Hub.



Local media reported in 2023 that the defendant in a trademark dispute case involving two pharmaceutical brands appealed after losing, saying that Chan copied the majority of the plaintiff’s written submission in his judgement.



That same year, Chan was also found to have plagiarised in most of his ruling in a case concerning real estate giant Great Eagle Holdings. The defendant, who lost the case, had filed an appeal accusing Chan of lifting large parts of the plaintiff’s submissions.



The appeal judges found that 92 per cent of Chan’s judgement was plagiarised. His judgement gave the impression that Chan had not exercised his responsibility and had unquestioningly accepted the submissions…

title: HKFP Lens: Bobby crowned champion at Hong Kong street dance contest

Hongkongers gathered for a dance-off final in Tsim Sha Tsui on Sunday, with Bobby, a dancer specialising in popping, winning the event.



Bobby at a dance-off final in Tsim Sha Tsui on July 19th, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.

Popping is known for its hip-hop-influenced jerky robotic movements.



A dance-off final in Tsim Sha Tsui on July 19th, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.

Siu Sa performs at a dance-off final in Tsim Sha Tsui on July 19th, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



Registered spectators voted on which dancers advanced to the next round.

title: Hong Kong issues 9 fines, 110 warnings over new construction site smoking ban
summary:
Hong Kong’s labour authorities have issued nine penalty tickets and 110 warnings since a citywide construction site smoking ban took effect last Friday, the labour commissioner has said.



A construction site. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



The enforcement action came as the authorities inspected 200 construction sites after the ban took effect, Commissioner for Labour Sam Hui told RTHK on Monday morning.



“Even if the evidence is indirect, or if we did not catch them in the act, as long as the information or evidence is sufficient to indicate they were smoking… we can issue a fine in the form of a fixed-penalty ticket,” Hui said.



The new rule was proposed and enacted in the wake of the Wang Fuk Court fire last November, which killed 168 people and displaced thousands. Investigations suggest that the blaze was likely caused by construction workers smoking at the estate, which was under renovation.



The ban designates all types of construction sites – including those related to building repair, maintenance or renovation – as no smoking areas. Offenders face a fixed-fine of HK$3,000.



Contractors responsible for construction works are required to ensure that no one smokes on their sites, with those failing to do so facing a maximum fine of HK$400,000.



Follow-up inspections



Hui said the authorities had issued nine fixed penalty tickets, while contractors were served four improvement notices and 110 written or verbal warnings.



A worker on the roof of Wang Cheong House, the first building to catch fire at Wang Fuk Court, on the day of the fire, dated November 26, 2025. Photo: CCTV footage via Wang Fuk Court independent committee.



For the four improvement notices, Hui said follow-up inspections would be conducted to check if the contractors had made the necessary rectifications, otherwise prosecutions may be initiated.



Hui also said that the industry had become more vigilant since the Wang Fuk Court fire, with many contractors installing surveillance ca…

title: Rubio in Philippines as US condemns ‘dangerous’ China actions
summary:
The United States condemned “dangerous and aggressive actions” by China following a clash with the Philippine navy in the South China Sea, as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Manila on Tuesday for a meeting of Southeast Asian nations.



US Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivers remarks to members of the media at the White House on May 5, 2026. Photo: The White House, via Flickr.



“China’s troubling pattern of provocations against the Philippines’ legitimate maritime operations undermines regional peace and stability and directly contradicts China’s repeated commitments to resolve disputes peacefully,” the US State Department said in a statement.



The US secretary of state landed in Manila on Tuesday morning for a meeting of his counterparts from the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).



While his entourage has not publicly confirmed talks with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, who will also be in Manila on Wednesday and Thursday, Rubio has said he is open to the possibility of a meeting.



The two met last year on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit in Kuala Lumpur and again in Munich in February.



In an op-ed published in Philippine media outlets Tuesday morning, Rubio heralded Washington’s commitment “to freedom of navigation in Southeast Asia” while reaffirming the US defensive umbrella in the region.



“This freedom is by no means guaranteed. If these waters were to fall under the control of a power willing to use trade as a geopolitical weapon, both the United States and the ASEAN states would face serious new threats to their sovereignty, security, and economic future,” he wrote, in a clear allusion to China.



Beijing claims sovereignty over almost the entire South China Sea, a vital global trade route, despite an international ruling that its claims have no legal basis.



Territorial claims in the South China Sea. Photo: Wikicommons.

title: Mentally impaired waiter jailed for 2 years and 4 months for inciting subversion by promoting pro-Taiwan party
summary:
A mentally impaired man has been jailed for two years and four months for inciting subversion by promoting a pro-Taiwan political party through online posts and putting up posters in public places



District Court. File photo: GovHK. 



Waiter Chan Ho-hin, 23, was sentenced at the District Court on Monday following his guilty plea earlier this month.



Judge Stanley Chan said the defendant’s offence spanned 10 months. During this time, he made posts on social media platforms and put up posters in public to promote the Taiwan-based Revive the Republic of China Freedom Party, according to local media.



The defendant admitted to putting up A4-sized posters relating to the party on the streets of Yau Ma Tei and Wong Tai Sin, as well as sending out application forms for people to join the group.



His posts on X included messages opposing the Chinese Communist Party and the protest slogan “Liberate Hong Kong, revolution of our times,” which has been declared illegal under the Beijing-imposed national security law.



Defence lawyers pleaded for leniency on the grounds that the defendant has a mild intellectual disability and that he was merely “parroting” the information he saw online.



Taiwan flag aboard the island’s coast guard vessel. Photo: Kuan Bi-ling, via Facebook.



Judge Chan accepted that the defendant’s mental condition might have impaired his political understanding, but said that the court must not treat national security risks lightly



He dismissed the defence’s argument that the defendant’s advocacy was “empty and vague,” saying that the 23-year-old had promoted ways of making petrol bombs in his social media posts.



Even though Hong Kong has entered a “different kind of atmosphere” since Beijing imposed the national security law in June 2020, potential security hazards still exist, the judge said.



He noted that the defendant did not show a high level of premeditation or have specific targets for incitement.



He ruled that the…

title: Taiwan says ‘significant’ rise in China maritime activity near island
summary:
Taiwan detected a sharp rise in the number of Chinese ships entering waters around the island democracy last month, a Taiwanese coast guard official said, as Beijing intensifies pressure on Taipei.



The Taiwan flag. Photo: Olaer/Elmer Anthony/Flickr.



China deploys military aircraft, warships and coast guard vessels around Taiwan on an almost daily basis to assert its claim of sovereignty over the island — which Taipei rejects.



Data show a “significant increase” in the number of Chinese ships conducting “grey zone harassment” in June, a Taiwan coast guard official said on the condition of anonymity in order to share the information with the media. The remarks were embargoed until Monday.



A total of 263 Chinese ships, including coast guard, rescue and research vessels, were detected in waters around Taiwan and its outer islands in June, compared with 200 a month earlier, and 171 in June 2025.



The figures do not include warships.



“Whether in terms of the types or the number of government vessels involved in these grey-zone activities, there was a significant increase,” the official told reporters.



The Taiwan Strait. Photo: U.S. Pacific Fleet, via Flickr CC2.0.



China launched “law enforcement” patrols in waters east of Taiwan last month, which Taipei has branded as “provocative” and “expansionism in disguise”.



Until June, China Coast Guard’s presence in the Western Pacific had been largely limited to participation in military drills around Taiwan.



During the operation, the China Coast Guard for the first time radioed cargo ships passing Taiwan for information about their crew and destination.



A senior government official said China’s aim was not only to disrupt shipping but to “prevent Taiwan from receiving supplies” by stopping commercial ships from entering its ports.



“What it is trying to do is put into practice what it h…

title: Hong Kong’s class of lawmakers head to Beijing for study tour in historic first
summary:
Hong Kong’s Legislative Council (LegCo) has headed to Beijing for a week-long study tour to learn about China’s development, the president of the legislature has said.



Hong Kong lawmakers taking a group photo before heading off to Beijing for a study tour on July 19, 2026. Photo: Starry Lee, via Facebook. 



Starry Lee, president of the Legislative Council, said in a Facebook post on Sunday that this is the first time an entire class of lawmakers has gone to Beijing together for a study tour.



“We are filled with anticipation. We will devote ourselves to our studies and make earnest observations,” Lee wrote in Chinese, adding that the trip was of “immense significance.”



All but one of the city’s 89 lawmakers are attending the trip. Legislator Ginny Wan did not join the Beijing tour, Sing Tao Daily reported.



The LegCo secretariat said in a reply to media outlets that Wan had notified president Lee of her absence in advance, and that Lee had accepted her explanation.



Wan, a lawyer and a Hong Kong deputy to the National People’s Congress of China, was selected a legislator in the Election Committee constituency in January.



Lawmaker Ginny Wan. Photo: Ginny Wan, via Facebook. 



A group photo taken of the lawmakers before they set off for the trip, posted by Starry Lee, showed six lawmakers missing. But local media reported that five of them traveled to Beijing themselves and later joined the rest of their colleagues.



There are currently 89 lawmakers in the legislature following William Wong’s resignation in early July. Wong, who was an Election Committee constituency lawmaker, stepped down from the post after his drink driving arrest.



‘A good time’ to learn about China



The LegCo president Lee said on Facebook that the legislature had done significant work over the past six months marking milestones of Hong Kong’s integration with China.

title: World Cup 2026: Tournament brought extra HK$500M revenue to Hong Kong’s bars and restaurants, industry rep says
summary:
The World Cup brought an additional HK$500 million in revenue to the city’s bars and restaurants, an industry rep has said, despite the time difference putting games in the middle of the Hong Kong night.



Lin Heung Tea House on July 5, 2026. Photo: Alexx_sze, via Threads.



Simon Wong, president of the Hong Kong Federation of Restaurants & Related Trades, said on an RTHK radio show on Monday morning that live screenings of the World Cup brought a higher-than-expected boost to eateries.



Revenue increased by around 6 per cent month-on-month, Wong said, much more than the 2 or 3 per cent initial forecast.



Lin Heung Tea House on July 5, 2026. Photo: Alexx_sze, via Threads.



“This is quite encouraging for the restaurant industry,” he said in Cantonese, adding that the atmosphere “heated up” as the World Cup reached the round of 16 and quarter-finals stages.



Wong’s comments were made just hours after Spain beat Argentina in the World Cup final, marking an end to the 104-match tournament.



This year’s World Cup was co-hosted by Canada, Mexico and the US, meaning matches were played in the middle of the night Hong Kong time due to a time difference of at least 12 hours.



Many bars and eateries – including famed yum cha restaurant Lin Heung Tea House in Central – set up large screens and extended their opening hours to cater to football fans.



Wong said that, with restaurants having invested in screens and other livestreaming hardware, he expected that eateries would capitalise on major sporting events to attract customers in the future.



Football fans watching the World Cup at Metro City Plaza in Tseung Kwan O on July 20, 2026. Photo: Metro City Plaza, via Facebook.



Beyond restaurants and bars, Hongkongers also packed shopping malls that were broadcasting the World Cup final in the early hours of Monday.

title: Pocket-size AI: Powerful phones star at China show
summary:
Tech firms are racing to roll out advanced smartphones that use artificial intelligence to do everything from ordering food to composing messages upon a simple voice command.



Humanoid robots from Booster Robotics play football during the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai on July 18, 2026. Photo: Hector Retamal/AFP.



Wide adoption of phones running on so-called AI agents would be a revolution, but would also take control away from major apps, which aren’t always happy about it.



At least three firm were showcasing so-called agentic phones at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai this weekend — heralding what may be to come.



Smartphone maker Nubia unveiled its NaviX Ultra, a phone powered by Doubao, China’s massively popular AI chatbot tool run by TikTok creator ByteDance.



“A new era of AI agent smartphones begins,” Nubia said, sharing images of the handsets online.



A limited run of a prototype dubbed the “Doubao Phone” sold out fast in December.



Initially, the prototype could follow simple voice commands to execute tasks across apps, including ordering food and comparing shopping prices.



However, days after it was released, tech giants including Alibaba, Tencent and JD.com restricted the built-in assistant’s access to their platforms.



Logo of Alibaba. File photo: Leon Lee, via Flickr CC2.0.



The move effectively disabled the phone’s AI agent, so ByteDance turned off the powerful tool in certain circumstances, including when payments were involved.



‘Lose control’



Gaining broad access to apps owned by other companies is a sticking point for AI agent devices, said Kiranjeet Kaur, associate research director at US market intelligence firm IDC.



Platforms want to keep direct contact with their users, otherwise “they lose control to another party”, she added.

title: ‘Pointless’: Tai Po fire survivors get no answers at owners’ meeting as gov’t buybacks loom
summary:
Residents of the Tai Po housing estate ravaged by last November’s deadly fire have received no answers at an owners’ meeting, as they face an imminent deadline to accept government buybacks of their units at Wang Fuk Court.



A woman guards the entrance as Wang Fuk Court residents attend a flat owners’ meeting at Tai Po Community Centre on July 19, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



Residents gathered on Sunday for the first general meeting of flat owners after the massive blaze tore through their estate, killing 168 people and displacing thousands. 



They had been calling for an owners’ meeting for months, but government-appointed estate administrators, Hop On Management, had cited difficulty in finding venues and verifying owners’ identity. Several residents deemed the meeting “pointless,” when speaking to reporters.



Wang Fuk Court residents attend a flat owners meeting at Tai Po Community Centre on July 19, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



On Sunday, the long-awaited meeting was held at community centres in Tai Po, Tin Shui Wai, Kai Tak and Wah Kwai via live broadcast and lasted almost six hours. Hop On reported on matters including insurance, refunds and the estate’s finances.



‘Evaded all questions’



However, some residents were frustrated by a lack of answers and left the gathering midway.



A Wang Kin House resident surnamed Chan left roughly two hours after the meeting started, saying that Hop On had “evaded all questions” posed by residents.



A Wang Fuk Court resident surnamed Chan leaves a flat owners’ meeting at Tai Po Community Centre on July 19, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



He said residents had asked why they were not allowed to return to their homes even though they had not sold their property titles.



“Which law in Hong Kong says we cannot go home?” Chan said to reporters in Cantonese. “I am the owner of the flat as long as I have not sold it, right?”

title: No plans to drop dog-friendly restaurant policy despite online backlash, Hong Kong minister says
summary:
There are no plans to halt a new policy allowing dogs to enter permitted Hong Kong restaurants and cafes, a minister has said amid online backlash.



Pet dogs inside Wan Land Mori cafe in Kowloon City on July 12, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



Tse Chin-wan, the environment and ecology minister, said on NowTV on Sunday that the policy is still in its “teething stage,” after it came into effect on July 9.



Backlash against the policy arose online after some people shared photos and complained about dog owners feeding their dogs with restaurant utensils, and allowing dogs on dining tables.



While some raised concerns of hygiene, others defended the policy, saying that dogs are not as dirty as one might assume. They said that those who dislike dogs can simply choose other restaurants that do not hold the dog-friendly permits.



“The photos shared by netizens are not fake; these incidents definitely happened. However, this is not a widespread issue. We hope that through our inspections and education, we can gradually eliminate non-compliant and improper behaviour during this adjustment period,“ Tse said in Cantonese.



He added that the government is only allowing a small number of restaurants to participate in the new scheme, which is a voluntary one. 



“Both the restaurants and the customers have a choice. Therefore, we see no need to halt the policy. We just need to learn as we go, and we will monitor the situation to see if improvements are needed in the future,” Tse said.



Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan meets the press on January 26, 2024. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



The official said authorities had granted 11 applications so far for restaurants that applied to quit the scheme.



The Hong Kong government issued licences to 940 restaurants and cafes under the scheme to welcome pet dogs in catering venues after receiving over 2,200 applications.

title: HKFP Lens: Hong Kong holds annual book fair as independent booksellers face exclusion, legal woes
summary:
Hong Kong’s book lovers are packing the city’s book fair, an annual event run by a government-established statutory body.



People attend the Hong Kong Book Fair in Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai, on July 17, 2026. The locations where booths of independent booksellers once stood have been turned into reading areas this year. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



The Hong Kong Trade Development Council (HKTDC) event took place in the backdrop of national security raids and arrests at two independent bookstores, while two others were reportedly banned from taking part in the fair.



On Wednesday, the first day of the fair, police searched Have a Nice Stay and Greenfield and arrested five operators were for alleged sedition.



People attend the Hong Kong Book Fair in Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai, on July 17, 2026. The locations where booths of independent booksellers once stood have been turned into reading areas this year. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



Last month, local media reported that bookstores Elmbook and Luck Win were disqualified by the fair’s organisers despite obtaining prior approval to participate.



The two long-running bookshops had been frequent exhibitors at the book fair. Both declined to comment, while the HKTDC said it would not discuss individual cases, according to local media.



Elmbook later announced the decision to shut down its 29-year-old physical store in Mong Kok and is holding a clearance sale.



A child wears a virtual reality headset at the Hong Kong Book Fair in Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai, on July 17, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



“Hundreds of boxes of new books have arrived in Hong Kong, and we look forward to welcoming book lovers for a treasure hunt,” it said.



At this year’s book fair, the booths that were previously assigned to Elmbook and Luck Win were turned into reading areas.

title: US ends its state of emergency over Hong Kong security threat
summary:
The United States has chosen not to extend its state of emergency over what it deemed threats posed by Beijing’s hardline national security law in Hong Kong, US officials confirmed Friday.



The White House. Photo: White House, via Flickr.



But it remains unclear whether Washington would restore preferential trade treatment for the financial hub — a move that had accompanied the July 2020 emergency declaration.



China’s Ministry of Commerce lauded the development, saying in a statement Friday that Washington’s move was “an important step in implementing the consensus reached during economic and trade talks between both sides.”



In 2020, during his first White House term, US President Donald Trump stripped Hong Kong of preferential trade treatment over Beijing’s clampdown on the city.



Trump declared a national emergency at the time, with an order saying that China’s actions to undermine Hong Kong’s autonomy contributed to an “unusual and extraordinary threat” to US national security.



Hong Kong in March 2025. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.



The order had been extended annually by the White House until now.



China’s Commerce Ministry said Friday that Washington recently confirmed to Beijing that the order would terminate.



But a US State Department spokesperson said although Trump allowed the national emergency to end, his earlier executive order “otherwise remains in effect.”



“Hong Kong is no longer sufficiently autonomous to justify differential treatment in relation to the PRC” under US laws and provisions listed in the order, the spokesperson added, referring to the People’s Republic of China.



A US Treasury Department spokesperson noted that 39 of 48 people impacted by the emergency’s expiration still face sanctions under a different act.



“The non-renewal is consistent with sanctions modernization efforts,” the Treasury spokespe…

title: China’s mega-oiler could break America’s Pacific base edge

Two tourists from Jilin province show their Xiaohongshu accounts on their mobile phones as they visit the Forbidden City in Beijing on July 11, 2026. Photo: Adek Berry/AFP.



The platform, which is reportedly preparing to file to go public as soon as this year, has shaken up the tourism industry in China, where domestic travel is booming to record levels.



Known as RedNote in English, Xiaohongshu’s interface is similar to the US social network Pinterest, but it is sometimes nicknamed “China’s Instagram” as users can post photos, videos and even livestream.



Travellers use the app to discover new destinations and plan their itineraries around photogenic locations, like the lake in the capital’s historic Shichahai area — one of many “daka” or “check-in” spots where Xiaohongshu is driving even more footfall.

Metres away, other photographers yelled instructions to ornately dressed young women who held their fingers in victory signs and arched their backs for the camera.



Li told AFP many of her competitors have a significant social media presence, including one who has 45,000 followers on Xiaohongshu and charges lower prices for photos.



Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote. Photo: Hillary Leung/HKFP.
